findings.claim: organisational design (Mintzberg's six structural types, mechanistic/organic continuum)
findings.failure_mode: Wrong author attached to the six structure types, repeated throughout this file (D003, D014, D020, D024, D028, D029, D033, D038, D039). The six types are the textbook's own list (Exhibit 4.6, adapted from Daft). In the deep ref Mintzberg is the managerial-roles author; the source cites Mintzberg (1979) only in an endnote for the broad mechanistic/organic split.
findings.evidence: Deep 189: 'Six organisational structure types span the mechanistic-organic continuum (Ch 4.3, Exhibit 4.6)', no author. Deep 33-41, 782: Mintzberg = role clusters. Source ~4660: Exhibit 4.6 'Adapted from: Daft, R., 2016, Organization Theory and Design'; source 4570 + endnote 21 (29108): Burns & Stalker; Mintzberg 1979; Emery & Trist, for mechanistic vs organic only.
findings.fix: correct: organisational design (six structure types, mechanistic/organic continuum)

findings.claim: four areas of the text are load-bearing in ways that other corpus sources do not duplicate. First, Chapter 4.3 supplies six organisational structure types ... Fourth ... Ch 18.6's treatment of explicit versus tacit knowledge — the corpus's only substantive treatment of the Nonaka-Takeuchi distinction
findings.failure_mode: Two false claims. OpenStax Organizational Behavior's deep ref carries the same six structure types, so the first area is duplicated. Nonaka and Takeuchi appear in neither this deep ref nor the converted source; the attribution is imported.
findings.evidence: openstax-organizational-behavior-deep 487: 'Six organisational structures along the mechanistic-to-organic continuum (Ch 15.3, Exhibit 15.6): functional → divisional → geographic → matrix → networked team → virtual'. 'Nonaka'/'Takeuchi': 0 hits in openstax-principles-management-deep and in the converted source. Deep 895: explicit vs tacit knowledge, no originator named.
findings.fix: correct: For software-business work, four areas of the text are load-bearing. First, Chapter 4.3 supplies six organisational structure types (functional, divisional, geographic, matrix, networked team, virtual) with explicit strength/weakness analysis (OB Ch 15.3 carries the same menu) ... Fourth, Ch 18.6's short treatment of *explicit* versus *tacit* knowledge is the citation for software-business questions about succession planning, knowledge transfer, contractor handoffs, and the cost of senior-engineer departures.

findings.claim: Environment-structure fit is not optional; mismatch produces structural drag.
findings.failure_mode: Hardens the source's position. The deep ref and source match structures to environments; the source also says the mechanistic form 'may still be relevant' and that not every part of an organisation needs an organic structure. 'Not optional' and 'structural drag' are the distillation's.
findings.evidence: Deep 187: mechanistic 'best suited' for stable/simple; organic 'work best' in unstable/complex. Source 4581-4596: 'this type of organizational design may still be relevant ... not every organization or every part of most organizations may require an organic type of structure'.
findings.fix: correct: The text treats environment-structure fit as the design question: which structure, for which part of the organisation, in which environment.

findings.claim: trying to combine cost leadership and differentiation produces firms "stuck in the middle" [V] that excel at neither.
findings.failure_mode: Hardens the source's hedge ('can lead to') into 'produces', and adds 'excel at neither'.
findings.evidence: Deep 410: 'Trying to combine [cost leadership and differentiation], Porter suggests, can lead to a firm being stuck in the middle' [V]. Source 12275.
findings.fix: correct: Porter's position: trying to combine cost leadership and differentiation 'can lead to a firm being stuck in the middle' [V].

findings.claim: Goal planning outperforms domain planning when the conditions support it.
findings.failure_mode: Adds a condition the source does not give; the source's finding is unconditional.
findings.evidence: Deep 829: 'Goal planning produces higher performance than domain planning' [BT]. Source 25946-25947: 'goal planning results in higher levels of performance than does domain planning alone'.
findings.fix: correct: Research cited by the text finds goal planning outperforms domain planning alone; domain planning is the fallback when goals cannot yet be set or agreed.

findings.claim: the more complex the change, the greater the need for involvement. (Source: Ch 17.2, Ch 17.7, Ch 17.8)
findings.failure_mode: Mis-cited: the complexity-involvement sentence is Ch 10.3 (managing change), not Ch 17.
findings.evidence: Deep 492: 'The more complex the potential change, the greater the need to involve employees in the process of planning and implementing change' [V] (Ch 10.3). Deep 861: Ch 17.8 control- vs involvement-oriented, no complexity sentence.
findings.fix: correct: ...approaches (Ch 17.8); separately, the change chapter holds that 'the more complex the potential change, the greater the need to involve employees' [V] (Ch 10.3). (Source: Ch 17.2, Ch 17.7, Ch 17.8, Ch 10.3)

findings.claim: This is the corpus's only substantive treatment of the Nonaka-Takeuchi distinction and the load-bearing citation for software-business succession planning...
findings.failure_mode: Nonaka-Takeuchi attribution is imported: neither the deep ref nor the source names them. The treatment is also one paragraph, and the Open Practice Library carries tacit-knowledge transfer practices, so 'only substantive treatment' overreaches.

findings.fix: correct: The text's explicit/tacit distinction (one paragraph in Ch 18.6) is the citation for software-business succession planning, contractor handoff, and senior-departure cost; the Open Practice Library carries the transfer practices (pairing, mobbing, mentorship).

findings.claim: The more complex the work, the greater the need for involvement. (Ch 17.8)
findings.failure_mode: The deep ref carries the complexity-involvement link only for change (Ch 10.3). Ch 17.8's own version (uncertainty and turbulence push planning and control toward the people doing the work) is in the converted source but not in the deep ref.
findings.evidence: Deep 492 (Ch 10.3); deep 861 (Ch 17.8) has no uncertainty link. Source 27227-27231: 'As organizations confront increasing environmental or technology-induced uncertainty, rapid environmental change, and turbulence, planning and controlling move closer to the point in the organization where the plans are implemented'.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to deep 861 'As organizations confront increasing environmental or technology-induced uncertainty, rapid environmental change, and turbulence, planning and controlling move closer to the point in the organization where the plans are implemented and carried out on a day-to-day basis' [V] (Ch 17.8). | correct: The more uncertain and turbulent the environment, the closer planning and control move to the people doing the work.

findings.claim: dominance (short-term win, long-term cost) ... Integration is strongest for ongoing high-stakes relationships.

Integration is the path Follett favours. | cycle-to-deep: add to deep 156 'Dominance is "impossible without incurring social costs in terms of a disaffected workforce" [V]; in a compromise "neither side is happy" [V] (Ch 3.6).'

findings.claim: Reward and coercive power produce compliance and alienation; rationality, expertise, and moralistic appeal produce commitment.

findings.fix: correct: Coercive power tends to alienate; reward power produces measured, 'what am I getting?' responses; rationality, expertise, and moralistic appeal produce commitment.

findings.section: Citation and Source-Integrity Notes, Borrowed-through gaps
findings.claim: Henry Mintzberg — six organisational structure types, three managerial role clusters, and the fragmented-manager-time findings are sourced [BT] (Ch 1.2; Ch 4.3; Ch 16.3). Mintzberg's The Nature of Managerial Work (1973) and Structure in Fives (1983) are the primary sources
findings.failure_mode: Six structure types are not Mintzberg's in the deep ref or source (D001). Structure in Fives is not cited by the source, and its typology is five configurations, not these six types. The role clusters and time findings are correctly Mintzberg's.
findings.evidence: Deep 33-41 (roles), 189 (six types, no author). 'Structure in Fives' 0 hits in source; source endnotes cite Mintzberg 1973, 1975, 1979, 1990, 2007, 2009.
findings.fix: correct: *Henry Mintzberg* — three managerial role clusters and the fragmented-manager-time findings are sourced [BT] (Ch 1.1; Ch 1.2; Ch 16.3), from *The Nature of Managerial Work* (1973) and later HBR work.

findings.section: Citation and Source-Integrity Notes, Evidence-marker continuity
findings.claim: Frameworks attributed to Mintzberg, ... Nonaka-Takeuchi ... are all [BT] in the deep reference ... [V]-marked source passages (the Drucker culture-and-strategy quote, the forced-ranking GE reversal passage, communication-as-invention framing) are paraphrased and cited by chapter.
findings.failure_mode: False on three counts: the deep ref carries no Mintzberg structures and no Nonaka-Takeuchi at all; the Drucker culture passage is quoted [V] at line 32, not paraphrased; communication-as-invention is quoted [V] at lines 126 and 173.
findings.evidence: Deep 189, 895 (no such attributions). Distillation 32, 126, 173 carry [V] quotations of those passages.
findings.fix: correct: Frameworks attributed to Porter, Cameron-Quinn, Taylor, Fayol, Weber, Hofstede, Follett, Drucker, and the motivation theorists are [BT] in the deep reference and attributed by name here. The Drucker culture passage (Key Concept 9), the rationality finding (Key Concept 13), communication-as-invention (Phase 6 and the worked example) and 'Documents take on lives of their own' are quoted [V] from the deep ref; the GE forced-ranking reversal is paraphrased. The worked example is operator-authored; its structural decisions trace to Ch 4.3 and its tacit-knowledge framing to Ch 18.6.
